items.prompt: Which term describes repeating back in your own words what a customer said to confirm you understood it?

options.label: Call deflection
Active listening
Escalation
Upselling

rubric: Paraphrasing to confirm understanding is a core part of active listening.
Escalation and upselling are different actions that do not check understanding.

items.prompt: What is the usual first step when answering a customer's phone call?

options.label: Ask for the customer's account number
Tell the customer the wait time
Offer a discount on the next order
Greet the customer and state your name

rubric: A greeting with your name opens the call politely and sets a professional tone.
Asking for account details comes after the greeting.

items.prompt: What does it mean to escalate a customer issue?

options.label: Offer a refund for the product
Close it without a reply to the customer
Ask the customer to call back later
Pass it to someone with more authority or expertise

rubric: Escalation means handing an issue to a higher level of authority or expertise.
Closing a ticket or offering a refund is not escalation.

items.prompt: What does the abbreviation FAQ stand for?

options.label: Fast answer queue
Formal account query
Frequently asked questions
First available quote

rubric: FAQ means frequently asked questions.
The other options are invented expansions.

items.prompt: Which of these is a written record of a customer's issue that is tracked until it is resolved?

options.label: A support ticket
A price list
A brochure
A marketing email

rubric: A ticket logs and tracks an issue to resolution.
The other items are not issue records.

items.prompt: Which of the following are customer service channels? Select all that apply.

options.label: Phone
Invoice template
Live chat
Email

rubric: Phone, chat and email are channels for contacting customers.
An invoice template is a document, not a channel.

items.prompt: A new support agent is told to follow the standard complaint steps. A customer calls upset about a late delivery. The agent wants to recall the usual first step in handling a complaint. Which step is it?

options.label: Transfer the call to a manager
Explain the company's delivery policy
Listen to the complaint without interrupting
Offer compensation right away

rubric: Listening fully comes first so the customer feels heard and the problem is clear.
Jumping to policy, compensation or transfer skips understanding the problem.

items.prompt: Why is it helpful to say "I understand this is frustrating" to an upset customer?

options.label: It tells the customer to calm down
It shows empathy so the customer feels heard
It ends the call faster by closing the issue
It admits the company is legally at fault

rubric: Empathy statements acknowledge feelings and help de-escalate.
They do not admit legal fault or order the customer to calm down.

items.prompt: Which reply is the best example of a positive tone in an email to a customer?

options.label: "That is not our problem."
"You should have read the policy first."
"We can't do anything about that."
"I can help with that. Here is what we will do."

rubric: Focusing on what you can do keeps the tone helpful.
The others blame or shut the customer down.

items.prompt: Why should an agent avoid jargon when explaining a fix to a customer?

options.label: Customers prefer very short replies
Jargon is against company law
Jargon makes replies take longer to send
The customer may not understand technical terms

rubric: Plain language ensures the customer can follow the fix.
The other reasons are not why jargon is avoided.

items.prompt: Which situation is an example of a customer complaint rather than a simple question?

options.label: A customer asks what time the store opens
A customer says an item arrived broken and wants it fixed
A customer asks if a product comes in blue
A customer asks how to reset a password

rubric: A complaint expresses dissatisfaction about a problem.
The others just request information.

items.prompt: Why is it better to set a clear timeframe, such as "within two business days", than to say "soon"?

options.label: It makes the promise legally binding
It sets expectations the customer can rely on
It lowers the number of tickets opened
It lets the agent avoid following up

rubric: Specific timeframes manage expectations and build trust.
Vague words leave customers unsure; timeframes do not remove follow-up duty.

items.prompt: Which actions help recover a customer after a company mistake? Select all that apply.

options.label: Apologise sincerely
Blame another department
Follow up to confirm the fix worked
Explain what will be done to fix it

rubric: Apology, a clear fix and follow-up rebuild trust.
Blaming others damages trust and avoids ownership.

items.prompt: A chat customer writes in capital letters that their order has not arrived and they are furious. The agent has no update yet. Which response best fits good service practice?

options.label: Close the chat and send a survey
Tell the customer to stop shouting in capitals
Say the delay is not the company's fault
Apologise, say you will check the order now and report back with a time

rubric: Apologising and committing to action calms the customer and keeps ownership.
Criticising, deflecting or closing the chat worsens the situation.

items.prompt: Why do customer service agents use active listening, such as paraphrasing, at the start of a phone complaint?

options.label: It mirrors the customer's anger so they feel you share it
It shortens the call by skipping the customer's background
It confirms the real problem before any fix is offered
It speeds up the script since the customer repeats details

rubric: Paraphrasing checks that you understood the actual issue before acting.
Distractors treat listening as a speed tool or as emotional mirroring, which misses its purpose.

items.prompt: Which customer message is best classified as a complaint rather than a question?

options.label: What time does the nearest store open on Sunday mornings?
My order arrived damaged for the second time this month.
Could you explain how the premium plan differs from the basic one?
How do I update the delivery address on my open order?

rubric: A complaint expresses dissatisfaction about something that went wrong.
The other options only request information or instructions.

items.prompt: A customer has a non-urgent problem, must send several screenshots and wants a written record of the exchange. Which channel suits this best?

options.label: Phone call
Email
Voicemail
Public social post

rubric: Email supports attachments, detail and a lasting record without urgency.
Phone and voicemail leave no written trail; a public post is not suited to private account details.

items.prompt: Why is it good practice to apologise to a customer even when the problem was not caused by you personally?

options.label: It acknowledges their frustration and helps move toward a solution
It admits legal liability so the customer is owed compensation
It shows the customer was wrong to expect a better experience
It closes the complaint so the ticket can be marked resolved

rubric: An apology recognises the customer's experience and lowers tension so you can solve the problem.
Distractors confuse an apology with admitting legal blame, closing the ticket or blaming the customer.

items.prompt: Why does telling a customer when they will next hear from you matter, even if the fix will take several days?

options.label: It proves the problem is already solved on the company's side
It lets you avoid giving any further updates until the fix is ready
It reduces anxiety and repeat contacts because they know what to expect
It removes the need to log the promise anywhere in the ticket history

rubric: Clear expectations on timing reduce uncertainty and chasing.
Distractors treat the promise as a way to stop updates or as proof of a fix.

items.prompt: Which of the following are signs that a customer feels they are not being heard? Select all that apply.

options.label: They say "As I already told your colleague..."
They ask "Are you even listening to me?"
They repeat the same point more loudly
They thank you and confirm the next step

rubric: Repetition, references to having already explained, and direct challenges signal feeling unheard.
Thanking you and confirming the plan signals the customer is satisfied with the exchange.

items.prompt: A customer writes in a live chat: "MY PARCEL IS A WEEK LATE AND NOBODY WILL TELL ME ANYTHING!!" The agent has not yet looked up the order. What is the best interpretation of this message and what it calls for?

options.label: The customer is likely frustrated, so acknowledge that feeling before explaining next steps
The customer typed by accident, so wait for a calmer message before replying
The customer is being abusive, so warn them about tone before continuing the chat
The customer wants compensation, so offer a voucher before checking any order details

rubric: Capitals and exclamation marks usually show strong frustration, which should be acknowledged first.
Distractors misread frustration as abuse, a compensation demand or a typing mistake.

items.prompt: Policy: faulty items can be refunded within 30 days with a receipt. A customer bought a kettle 12 days ago, has the receipt, and says it stopped heating. What should you do?

options.label: Ask them to wait for a supplier report before any decision is made
Pass the case to a manager, because every refund needs approval
Offer the refund under the 30-day policy and explain how it is paid
Offer store credit only, because the kettle has already been opened

rubric: The case meets every condition of the stated policy, so the refund applies directly.
Distractors invent extra restrictions or approval steps that the policy does not include.

items.prompt: A caller has just finished explaining that they were charged twice for the same subscription. Using the steps listen, acknowledge, act, what should you say next?

options.label: "Please hold while I find out which department is to blame for this error."
"I'll add a discount to your account before I confirm what was charged."
"I'm sorry about the double charge; I'll check it now and arrange a correction."
"Our billing system sometimes processes payments twice, which is why this happens."

rubric: After listening, the next step is to acknowledge the problem and state the action you will take.
Distractors explain the cause first, focus on blame, or offer a discount before checking facts.

items.prompt: A customer has been waiting two weeks for a refund. Which email opening best applies good recovery practice?

options.label: "Refunds can take up to 14 working days, as stated in our policy."
"I'm sorry your refund is late. I've checked, and it will reach you by Friday."
"Thank you for contacting us. Your query has been received."
"We note your complaint and will respond in due course."

rubric: Good recovery apologises, shows you have acted and gives a concrete date.
Distractors are policy-quoting, generic or vague and give no ownership or timeline.

items.prompt: You may refund up to 100 dollars. A customer with a valid complaint asks for a 250 dollar refund. What is the best next step?

options.label: Ask them to call back tomorrow and try a different agent
Escalate to a supervisor and tell the customer what happens next and when
Approve the full amount to avoid making the customer wait
Say the request is not possible and end the conversation politely

rubric: Requests beyond your authority should be escalated with clear communication of the next step and timing.
Distractors exceed authority, refuse without help, or push the work back onto the customer.

items.prompt: You have just fixed a customer's login problem in a live chat. Which closing message is best?

options.label: "Your account is working now. Is there anything else I can help with today?"
"Done. This chat will close automatically in two minutes."
"Please fill out our survey; your feedback decides my performance rating."
"Glad that's fixed. Contact us again only if it breaks a second time."

rubric: A good close confirms the outcome and offers further help.
Distractors are abrupt, pressure the customer for a survey, or discourage future contact.

items.prompt: You promise a customer you will call back at 3 pm with an update, but you have no news yet. Which actions apply good practice? Select all that apply.

options.label: Call at 3 pm anyway and say what you are still waiting on
Tell the customer who will be calling them back
Record the promised callback time in the ticket
Wait for the customer to ring in if there is no news

rubric: Logging the promise, calling on time even without news, and naming the caller keep the commitment reliable.
Waiting for the customer to call breaks the promise and leaves them uncertain.

items.prompt: A caller waited 40 minutes on hold. When connected, they only ask what time your store closes on Saturday. The queue behind them is still long. What should you do?

options.label: Answer in one word without comment to keep the call short for others
Explain that staffing shortages caused the long wait before answering
Apologise for the wait, give the closing time clearly, and ask if they need anything else
Offer a voucher at once before you know whether they had other problems

rubric: Acknowledge the wait, answer the question clearly, and check for other needs.
Distractors make excuses, ignore the experience, or offer compensation unprompted.

items.prompt: A customer emails to complain that their order is five days late. You have confirmed it is held at a depot and will be delivered in two days. Which opening reply best applies the acknowledge, apologise, act sequence?

options.label: Thank you for your patience. Your order is in transit and you will receive tracking updates by email shortly.
I understand you're upset. Could you please confirm your order number and address again so I can look into this?
I'm sorry your order is late. It is held at a depot, I've flagged it, and delivery is now due in two days.
Delivery dates are estimates under our terms, and depot delays are outside our control, but it should arrive in two days.

rubric: The key acknowledges the problem, apologises and states a concrete action and date.
Distractors lean on policy, re-ask for details already known, or give vague reassurance with no specifics.

items.prompt: On a call, a customer spends two minutes explaining a billing problem with several details and rising frustration. What should you do first before proposing a fix?

options.label: Summarise the problem in your own words and ask them to confirm you have it right.
Apologise and transfer them to the billing team to save time.
Start checking the account while they talk so you can offer a fix as soon as they stop.
Explain the billing policy so they understand why the charge may have appeared.

rubric: Summarising and confirming checks understanding and shows the customer they were heard.
Distractors skip confirmation, jump to policy, or hand off prematurely.

items.prompt: In a live chat, you need about four minutes to look up a customer's warranty details in another system. What is the best way to handle that wait?

options.label: Send a short message with the reason and an estimate, then check back if it runs longer.
Ask the customer to try again later when the system may be faster.
Send a series of quick filler messages so the chat looks active.
Stay silent until you have the answer so you only send accurate information.

rubric: Telling the customer what you are doing and for how long manages the wait.
Silence, deflection and filler messages all leave the customer uninformed or unhelped.

items.prompt: Your authority lets you approve refunds up to $50. A customer with a clearly valid claim asks for an $80 refund. What should you do?

options.label: Hand the case to a supervisor with a full summary and tell the customer what happens next and when.
Tell the customer the claim cannot be processed and to contact support again later.
Offer $50 and explain that this is the most that can be done.
Approve two separate refunds of $40 so the customer is satisfied quickly.

rubric: Escalating with a summary avoids repeating the story and keeps the customer informed.
Splitting refunds bypasses controls; partial offers and deflection fail a valid claim.

items.prompt: A customer emails three separate questions: how to change their address, when their invoice is due, and how to cancel. Which reply structure is best?

options.label: Answer each question in the order asked, using numbered points, and invite follow-up.
Reply to the cancellation question first, since it is the most important to the business.
Write one paragraph covering everything and let the customer pick out what they need.
Answer the address question in detail and add a link to the help centre for the rest.

rubric: Answering every question clearly in order makes the reply easy to use.
Distractors leave questions unanswered, bury the answers, or put business priorities first.

items.prompt: You are closing a call where a complaint was resolved with a replacement item to be shipped. Which actions should be part of the close? Select all that apply.

options.label: Give a case reference number and ask if anything else is needed.
Recap what was agreed and the delivery timeframe.
End the call quickly to keep your handle time low.
Promise the replacement will definitely arrive tomorrow to reassure them.

rubric: Recapping the agreement and giving a reference with a check for other needs confirms resolution.
Promising unverifiable dates and rushing the close create new problems.

items.prompt: A customer was charged twice for a monthly subscription. You verify the duplicate charge and can issue a refund, which the bank usually takes 5 to 7 business days to show. The customer is annoyed and asks what happens now. Which response best applies service recovery?

options.label: Explain that duplicate charges sometimes happen with automatic billing and that a refund is being processed.
Apologise, confirm the refund amount, state the 5 to 7 day timeframe, and send written confirmation.
Apologise, say you will refund immediately, and ask them to wait for the next statement to see it.
Apologise, say the money will be back shortly, and advise them to contact their bank if it is not.

rubric: The key sets accurate expectations and gives written proof of the action.
Distractors are vague, explain rather than recover, or promise something that will not happen.

items.prompt: A support team's first response time is excellent, yet customer satisfaction scores are falling. Which metric would best help diagnose the cause?

options.label: Average handle time per conversation
First contact resolution rate
Number of contacts received per day
Percentage of agents meeting their schedule

rubric: Fast replies that don't solve problems cause repeat contacts, which first contact resolution reveals.
Other metrics measure speed, volume or adherence, not whether issues get resolved.

items.prompt: An agent gives a customer a correct, policy-based answer about a refused return. The customer says, "You people never listen." What is the most likely cause of that reaction?

options.label: The agent gave the policy without acknowledging the customer's specific situation.
The answer was delivered too slowly for the customer to follow.
The policy is wrong, so the customer is rightly dissatisfied.
The customer is deliberately being difficult and would not accept any answer.

rubric: A correct answer with no acknowledgement of the customer's circumstances feels like not being heard.
Distractors blame the customer, the policy or speed without evidence.

items.prompt: Contacts about invoices doubled the week after a redesigned billing email was sent. Tags show most customers ask what a new line item means. What is the most likely root cause?

options.label: Agents are not trained well enough to answer invoice questions.
Customers are receiving their invoices later than before.
Customers are more likely to complain in that week of the month.
The new email does not explain the line item clearly enough.

rubric: Timing after the change and the common question point to unclear content in the email.
Other causes don't fit the pattern of one repeated question.

items.prompt: In a transcript, the agent apologises, says "unfortunately that is our policy" about a refused exchange, and ends the chat. The customer escalates. Which step in the conversation is the main fault?

options.label: Citing the policy, because policies should never be mentioned to customers.
Apologising, because it implies the company was at fault.
Using the word "unfortunately", because it sounds negative.
Ending the chat without offering any alternative or next step after the refusal.

rubric: Refusing without alternatives leaves the customer stuck, prompting escalation.
Apologising and explaining a policy are fine; wording alone is not the main problem.

items.prompt: One agent has the shortest average handle time on the team but also the highest repeat-contact rate. What is the most plausible interpretation?

options.label: The agent is closing conversations before confirming the customer's issue is fully resolved.
The agent is the most efficient and the repeat contacts come from difficult customers.
The agent is spending too long on each customer and causing follow-ups.
The agent's metrics are unreliable and should be ignored.

rubric: Short calls plus many repeats suggest speed is being prioritised over resolution.
Other options ignore the pairing of low handle time and high repeats.

items.prompt: Which observations suggest a complaint stems from a process or product problem rather than an individual agent's mistake? Select all that apply.

options.label: Complaints jump right after a system release.
Many customers raise the same complaint across different agents.
Different agents give customers conflicting answers to the same question.
Only one agent's customers raise the complaint.

rubric: Patterns across agents, timing with changes, and inconsistent answers point to systemic causes.
Complaints concentrated on one agent point to an individual issue.

items.prompt: A customer thanked an agent for a refund, then left a one-star review. Records show the agent promised the refund within 3 to 5 days; it arrived after 12 days because of a bank delay the agent did not mention. What best explains the review?

options.label: The refund process itself was faulty and should have been cancelled.
The agent should have refused to give any timeframe.
The customer was never going to be satisfied and the thanks was insincere.
The agent set an expectation that did not account for the usual delay, so the late refund felt like a broken promise.

rubric: An over-optimistic timeframe turned a normal delay into a broken promise.
Other options blame the customer or propose unrealistic fixes rather than the expectation gap.

items.prompt: After a coaching push, a chat team's average handle time fell 15%, but CSAT dropped and repeat contacts within 48 hours rose. What is the most likely explanation?

options.label: The CSAT survey wording must have changed, since handle time cannot possibly influence repeat contact volume
Customers are now contacting support about much harder issues, which naturally lowers their satisfaction scores
Agents are closing chats faster without confirming the problem is solved, so issues come back
Shorter chats always reduce satisfaction because customers judge how much a company cares by chat length

rubric: Faster closing without confirmation explains falling CSAT and rising repeats together.
Distractors assume unsupported changes or treat length as the cause.

items.prompt: A customer emails three times in a week, getting terser each time. Each reply came from a different agent and answered only the latest message. What is the root cause?

options.label: Response times are too slow, because each reply took longer to arrive than the first-reply target
Replies treat each email as a new question, so the underlying unresolved problem is never addressed
The customer sends too many emails, which should be limited by a policy of one message per week
Agents lack politeness training, so the tone of their replies is what keeps provoking the customer

rubric: Fragmented handling with no case continuity leaves the real issue untouched.
Distractors blame tone, volume or speed, none of which the scenario shows.

items.prompt: A caller says, 'I've explained this twice already,' right after a transfer to billing. The first agent had only said, 'I'll pass you over.' Which part of the process most likely failed?

options.label: The customer should have been told that transfers always require restating the issue for security reasons
The first agent should have handled every billing issue personally instead of transferring any call to another team
The transfer passed on no case summary, so the customer had to restate the problem to the next agent
The billing agent should have put the customer on hold to read the notes aloud and ask for confirmation

rubric: A cold transfer without context handoff forces repetition.
Distractors ignore the missing handoff or invent a security rationale.

items.prompt: A customer says a refund promised 'within 5 to 7 business days' hasn't arrived 10 days after they asked. Which detail should the agent check first?

options.label: The customer's tone in the message, since angry customers tend to overstate how long they have been waiting
Whether the customer's bank is large, since large banks tend to process refunds more slowly than small banks
Whether the customer has contacted support before, since repeat callers often misjudge how long they have waited
The date the refund was actually issued, since the promised window and the customer's wait start at different points

rubric: The window runs from issue date, not request date, so the timeline must be reconciled first.
Distractors rely on stereotypes about customers or banks.

items.prompt: A QA review finds an agent scores top marks for empathy phrases yet has the team's lowest first-contact resolution. What does this pattern most likely show?

options.label: The QA form is invalid, because empathy should never be scored separately from average handle time
Empathy wording is delivered as a script, while diagnosing and fixing the customer's issue gets less attention
Empathy and resolution are opposed skills, so a high score in one guarantees a low score in the other
The agent is working the hardest queue, so the resolution rate needs no further investigation at all

rubric: Scripted empathy with weak problem-solving matches high empathy scores and low resolution.
Distractors claim a false trade-off or dismiss the data without evidence.

items.prompt: Which findings point to a product or knowledge-base problem rather than individual agent performance? Select all that apply.

options.label: One agent's reopen rate is double the team average across all topics
Contacts about one setting jumped across all agents after a release
Tenured and new agents alike show low first-contact resolution on that topic
One agent's CSAT dipped during a week of schedule changes
Customers quote the same unclear instruction from a help article

rubric: Patterns spread across agents and tied to shared content or releases indicate a systemic cause.
Single-agent anomalies point to individual or local factors.

items.prompt: A customer emails: 'Your technician was rude and fixed nothing.' The job record shows the technician replaced the router as requested and closed the job as resolved. The customer's original complaint was dropped connections in the back bedroom. What does the evidence most strongly suggest?

options.label: The router replacement was unnecessary, so the technician should be charged for the extra visit and parts
The technician was rude, and that rudeness is the only reason the customer reports the fix as failed
The job was closed against the listed task, not the customer's real problem, which likely remains unresolved
The customer is exaggerating, because the record proves the work was completed correctly and professionally

rubric: Closing against the task rather than the symptom explains 'fixed nothing' despite a completed record.
Distractors dismiss the customer or jump to blame without evidence.

items.prompt: A parcel arrived four days late, spoiling a time-sensitive gift. Criteria: proportionate cost, clear ownership, no promise you cannot keep. Which recovery is best?

options.label: Apologise for the specific impact, refund shipping, and add a modest credit, all confirmed in one message
Explain that the carrier caused the delay and offer nothing further, since the company was not at fault
Refund the entire order and add a large voucher, so the customer cannot possibly remain unhappy with us
Apologise and promise that every future order will arrive on time, so the customer regains full confidence

rubric: It is proportionate, owns the impact and promises only what can be delivered.
Distractors overpromise, overcompensate or deflect ownership.

items.prompt: A customer's payment failed twice and they are angry. Criteria: acknowledge the impact, take ownership, give a concrete next step. Which reply best meets all three?

options.label: I understand how frustrating this is. I'm checking your account now and will email you the result within one hour.
I'm sorry for the trouble. Payments sometimes fail, so please try again later and contact us if it keeps happening.
Thank you for your patience. Our system processes payments reliably, so the issue is most likely on your card's side.
I sincerely apologise for any inconvenience this may have caused and appreciate your valued custom as our customer.

rubric: It acknowledges impact, takes ownership and sets a specific time-bound step.
Distractors push work to the customer, shift blame or stay vague.

items.prompt: A lead is choosing chat concurrency. Criteria: protect CSAT on complex billing disputes, use idle time on simple FAQ chats. Which policy is best?

options.label: Allow up to three on simple FAQ chats, but cap at one during a billing dispute
Allow three chats per agent at all times, since idle time between customer replies is the main cost to remove
Limit every agent to one chat at a time, because quality always falls whenever attention is shared at all
Let each agent choose concurrency freely, because agents know their own capacity better than any rule does

rubric: Concurrency varies by complexity, matching both stated criteria.
Distractors apply one blanket rule or ignore the stated criteria.

items.prompt: A customer returns a defective blender two days after the 30-day window and has bought regularly for years. Criteria: fairness, limited precedent, cost. Which decision is best?

options.label: Approve and log it as a defect exception, since the fault is ours and that reason limits precedent
Approve because of loyal purchase history, telling the customer that loyalty earns flexibility on deadlines
Offer a partial refund of half the price, since splitting the cost is a fair compromise for both sides
Refuse, because any exception to a stated deadline invites every customer to demand the same treatment

rubric: A defect-based, documented exception is fair and sets a narrow precedent.
Distractors ignore the defect or tie the exception to loyalty or arbitrary splitting.

items.prompt: A manager plans to rank agents solely on monthly CSAT. Which is the strongest criticism of this plan?

options.label: Few customers respond and scores reflect factors agents can't control, so the ranking is unreliable
Rankings demotivate agents, so no individual measure should ever be used to assess their performance
CSAT really measures speed rather than quality, so handle time would be a better single measure of agents
CSAT is always inaccurate because customers rarely tell the truth in surveys about the service they got

rubric: Low, self-selected response and outside influences make a single-metric ranking unreliable.
Distractors overgeneralise or swap in another single metric.

items.prompt: You must decline a customer's demand for a refund outside policy. Which elements make the refusal more likely to preserve the relationship? Select all that apply.

options.label: Suggest the customer misread the terms
Offer the closest alternative you are allowed to give
Apologise several times so the decision feels softer
State the next step and who owns it
Explain the purpose behind the rule, not just its number

rubric: Rationale, a permitted alternative and a clear next step keep the customer respected and informed.
Repeated apologies and implied blame weaken trust.

items.prompt: A customer whose repair was delayed twice threatens a harsh public review unless given a full refund. Policy allows repair-delay credits up to 20%. Criteria: be honest, don't reward threats, fix the real problem. Which response is best?

options.label: Warn that threats of reviews may lead to account closure, then process the repair in the standard way
Ignore the review threat, offer the repair again in the usual queue, and wait for the customer to calm down
Grant the full refund immediately, since a public review would cost more than the repair fee does
Give a firm repair date with a named owner and the standard 20% credit, without referring to the review

rubric: It fixes the problem, stays within policy and treats the customer the same regardless of the threat.
Distractors reward the threat, escalate hostilities or neglect the delay.

items.prompt: A retailer's average order is $20. Investigating a 'not received' claim costs about $12 in agent time, and only about 3% of such claims are fraudulent. Criteria: total cost and long-term loyalty. Which policy is best?

options.label: Ask the customer to wait seven days before any action, because many parcels turn up late on their own
Refund or reship automatically under a value threshold, and audit patterns of repeat claimants afterwards
Investigate every claim with carrier proof first, because any unverified refund invites more fraud later
Offer a small credit on every claim, because it saves investigation cost and cuts the refund payout

rubric: Investigation costs more than the expected fraud loss, so automatic remedy plus pattern audits is cheapest and protects loyalty.
Investigate-everything ignores cost; blanket credits and forced waiting both irritate genuine customers.

items.prompt: A team scripts 'I completely understand how frustrating this is' as the opener for every contact. CSAT has dropped on complex cases. Which critique is best supported by the criterion of perceived sincerity?

options.label: Empathy lines delay resolution; agents should skip acknowledgement and go straight to the technical fix
Generic empathy reads as scripted; acknowledgement works better when it names the customer's specific problem and impact
The phrase is too weak; agents should apologise more strongly and more often to show the company takes blame
The problem is the channel; empathy statements only work by phone, so chat and email should drop them entirely

rubric: Identical wording on every contact signals insincerity; specific acknowledgement shows real listening.
Other options either escalate the scripting, wrongly blame the channel, or discard acknowledgement altogether.

items.prompt: Criteria: irreversibility and scale of harm. A support lead ranks four risks. Which should rank highest?

options.label: Agents give slightly different goodwill credits for similar delays across shifts on the same day
Agents forget to send the satisfaction survey link after about one in ten resolved chats
Agents sometimes exceed the 8-minute handle-time target during complex billing calls
Agents skip identity checks on a caller who sounds distressed and claims urgent account access need

rubric: Skipping verification can expose personal data or enable account takeover, which cannot be undone.
The other risks are real but are recoverable, low-impact or merely inconsistent.

items.prompt: A B2B support team is judged mainly on average handle time (AHT), and it has fallen 15% in a quarter. Reopened tickets rose 30%. Which judgement is most defensible?

options.label: The AHT target is working, since faster contacts free capacity and reopens are a normal cost of speed
Reopens come from bad products rather than agents, so the metric mix needs no change and no coaching
AHT is being met by premature closure; pair it with first-contact resolution and reopen rate as joint measures
Reopens show customers are over-contacting; the team should add a self-service article for every ticket type

rubric: Rising reopens alongside falling AHT suggests tickets are closed before being solved; balanced measures remove that incentive.
Other options defend the metric, misread the cause or deflect responsibility.

items.prompt: 'The customer is always right' is standard advice. Criteria: staff wellbeing, fairness to other customers and retention. In which case does the advice most clearly break down?

options.label: A customer is confused by a bill and insists the charge is wrong before checking the details
A customer complains in public reviews about slow replies that were genuinely slower than promised
A customer misreads a clearly stated return window and asks for a one-off exception
A customer repeatedly insults an agent by phone while demanding a refund that policy allows

rubric: Abuse warrants a boundary-setting step even when the underlying claim is valid, to protect staff; resolve the claim but warn about conduct.
The other cases are ordinary disagreements or valid complaints where openness serves the customer.

items.prompt: Criteria: customer risk and the agent's authority. Which situations justify escalating to a senior or specialist instead of continuing at tier 1? Select all that apply.

options.label: The customer threatens legal action over a disputed contract term
The customer asks for a refund that tier 1 can approve under policy
The customer sounds irritated but the fix is within the agent's authority
The customer asks the same question twice because they missed the first answer
The customer reports a possible safety hazard with a product they bought

rubric: Safety hazards and legal threats carry risks beyond tier 1 authority and need specialist handling.
Irritation, repeat questions and in-policy refunds are routine for tier 1.

items.prompt: After a 6-hour outage, a long-standing customer demands a full year's fee refund. Policy caps outage credit at one week. You can't approve more. Criteria: keep trust, avoid unfair precedent, stay within authority. Which response is best?

options.label: Refuse, restate the one-week cap, and close the ticket since policy gives you no discretion
Offer a vague promise that the company will look at it, and avoid quoting any figure or date
Apply the one-week credit now, explain why, and submit the larger request for exception review with a timeline
Grant the year's refund quietly to keep the customer, and note it as a one-off for the record

rubric: It delivers what you may give, is honest about limits, and routes the exception request properly with a clear follow-up.
Others breach authority and create precedent, stonewall, or leave the customer uncertain.

items.prompt: A delivery delay hits 5,000 customers. Constraints: contact within 24 hours, compensation at most 10% of order value, no spike in inbound calls. Which recovery design meets all of them?

options.label: Post a delay banner on the website and hold email until new delivery dates are confirmed for everyone
Send proactive notices with a new date, an automatic 10% credit, and a self-serve link to cancel or reroute
Phone every affected customer in order of order value and offer individual compensation up to 25%
Wait for customers to contact support, then give each caller a 10% credit after verifying their order

rubric: Proactive contact, capped automatic credit and self-service address timing, budget and call volume together.
Others wait for inbound contact, exceed the cap, or miss the 24-hour contact limit.

items.prompt: Design a routing rule. Constraints: urgent outage reports reach an engineer in 15 minutes, routine questions stay with tier 1, and customers never have to pick their own priority. Which design fits?

options.label: Detect outage keywords and affected-service data on intake, route matches to an engineer queue with a 15-minute alert
Let customers choose a 'severity' menu option and route the highest choice to engineers directly
Route by arrival time, with the first ten contacts each hour going to engineers and the rest to tier 1
Route all contacts to engineers first, who then pass routine ones down to tier 1 after reading them

rubric: Automatic detection removes customer self-rating and sends only urgent items to engineers.
Self-selected severity breaks the constraint; the other designs waste engineers or ignore urgency.

items.prompt: Design a QA scorecard. Constraints: it must be fair across phone, chat and email, reward real resolution, and resist agents gaming it with scripted phrases. Which is best?

options.label: Score on customer survey results alone, since they reflect what customers actually felt in each case
Score on required phrases for greeting, empathy and closing, with each weighted equally across channels
Score outcomes and accuracy against channel-adjusted criteria, with calibrated reviewers sampling cases and giving coaching notes
Score on speed alone, with channel-specific time targets, since speed is easy to measure fairly

rubric: Outcome-focused, channel-adjusted criteria with calibration meet fairness and anti-gaming constraints.
Phrase checklists invite scripting; speed ignores resolution; survey-only is noisy and uneven by channel.

items.prompt: A team proposes this post-incident plan: publish a status page, email all affected customers once the fix is live, and brief agents with a script. What is the most important thing it is missing?

options.label: A longer status-page history so that future customers can see past incidents of this kind
A promise of compensation announced in advance of knowing the incident's cost to customers
A way to reach customers who already contacted support, with their open cases updated and closed individually
A plan for agents to apologise personally by phone to every customer, regardless of impact

rubric: Customers with open cases need follow-up on their own tickets, or they must chase; the plan treats everyone as a generic audience.
Other options are excessive, cosmetic or financially premature.

items.prompt: Redesign a help centre. Constraints: top-20 questions drive 60% of contacts, content must stay accurate after product changes, and agents need one source. Which plan meets all?

options.label: Replace the help centre with a chatbot trained once on past tickets and not updated afterward
Write articles for the top 20 questions, assign owners tied to product releases, and have agents use the same articles
Rewrite all 800 articles at once and review them each year before the annual product launch
Let each agent keep a private notes file for fast answers, and share the best items every quarter

rubric: Focuses on high-volume content, ties ownership to releases for accuracy, and uses one shared source.
Others are unfocused, fragment sources, or go stale.

items.prompt: Design a chat-to-phone handoff. Constraints: customers never repeat their story, identity is not re-verified needlessly, and the phone agent can see what was promised. Which elements must it include? Select all that apply.

options.label: A requirement that the customer reads out their case history at the start of the call
A rule that the phone agent restarts troubleshooting to confirm the chat steps
A case summary with the issue, steps tried and any commitments made in chat
A flag showing identity already verified in chat, with the method used

rubric: A summary with commitments and a verification flag meet all three constraints.
Restarting troubleshooting and having customers recount history both force repetition.

items.prompt: After a product recall, contacts will triple for three weeks. Constraints: no new hires, safety questions answered within an hour, routine status queries must not block them. Which plan fits?

options.label: Create a safety-priority queue with trained agents, automate recall-status lookups, and move other work to later times
Spread all agents evenly across every contact type and rely on overtime to clear the backlog
Send agents a short FAQ and ask customers to wait for replies in arrival order across channels
Pause email and chat for the period so everyone can answer calls, where urgency is easiest to judge

rubric: A dedicated safety queue plus automation of status queries protects the one-hour limit without extra headcount.
Others fail to separate urgent from routine or remove channels customers need.
